subtitle: When someone tells you an action caused harm, start by receiving the concern. Then look at the specific action and its effect, and plan an appropriate response that includes responsibility and follow-through.
scope: For leaders, supervisors, and team leads responding to a person who describes an action or interaction as harmful. Acknowledging a concern is not an investigative finding. This course does not require personal disclosure, forgiveness, mediation, or a private resolution before formal reporting. State reporting, conduct, privacy, safety, and employment responsibilities remain applicable. Cases are practice.
introTranscript: When someone says an action was harmful, a leader may feel pressure to defend intent, settle the facts immediately, or produce an apology that ends the conversation. A more useful response makes room to understand the specific concern and identifies what responsibility follows. This course examines a practice project discussion in which a supervisor publicly dismisses an employee’s access concern. You will practice receiving feedback, distinguishing purpose from effect, clarifying without interrogation, taking responsibility for a specific action, choosing appropriate routes, and checking whether a repair changed the work. The course does not promise restored trust or treat the person’s willingness to forgive as a measure of success.

intro.heading: Receive the concern without making reassurance the first task
intro.body:
Hearing that an action was harmful can bring discomfort, surprise, or disagreement. Those reactions do not need to become the person’s problem to solve. Pause, acknowledge that a concern has been raised, and identify a suitable way to understand it. Avoid demanding immediate reassurance that you are a good person or that the relationship is fine.

In a practice DHS project meeting, a supervisor publicly calls an access concern a distraction. Later, the employee says the comment was harmful because it made a work-related question seem illegitimate. The supervisor can recognize the concern and the specific comment without announcing an investigative conclusion or promising that every interpretation is settled.

A useful first response is bounded and professional: acknowledge the comment being discussed, state that the effect needs attention, and explain the next appropriate step. If the substance requires a formal route, fulfill that responsibility promptly. Do not make the employee complete an informal explanation or calm the supervisor before the concern can be received.

flashcards.back: The purpose someone had in taking an action; it does not by itself establish the effect.
The effect of an action on participation, work, access, or experience.
Recognizing that a concern has been raised and deserves an appropriate response.
Identifying what action or duty is yours to address without deciding matters outside your authority.
A specific action intended to address an effect or prevent recurrence; its usefulness needs review.
The applicable authorized process for a concern requiring reporting, investigation, safety, or another responsibility.

items.title: Acknowledgment
items.body: Recognize the specific concern instead of offering a general statement of good intentions. In the meeting case, the supervisor can name the dismissal of the access question and agree to examine its effect. This shows attention without inventing facts, declaring a legal finding, or promising an outcome outside the supervisor’s role.

items.title: Defensiveness
items.body: A request for reassurance can shift the burden to the employee. Asking whether the supervisor is still trusted or respected makes the conversation about the supervisor’s self-image. Keep attention on the action, the work effect, and the appropriate next responsibility rather than requiring the person to make the situation comfortable.

items.title: Finding and duty
items.body: Acknowledgment and an authorized finding are different. The supervisor can receive a report and take relevant action while facts remain unsettled. If the concern includes an allegation requiring immediate reporting, uncertainty does not remove that duty. Explain the route and limits rather than make receipt depend on a completed private investigation.

tabs.label: Intent defense
tabs.body: An intent defense can be relevant later, but using it first can leave the described effect unexamined. “I meant well” does not answer whether the access concern was dismissed. Acknowledge the action and effect before explaining context, without making intent a reason to close the concern.

tabs.label: Bounded acknowledgment
tabs.body: A bounded acknowledgment recognizes what is being raised and identifies an appropriate next step. It does not require agreeing to every interpretation or announcing a finding. It allows the leader to remain accurate while responding professionally and fulfilling relevant duties.

tabs.label: Reassurance request
tabs.body: A reassurance request can pressure the person to soften or retract feedback to protect the relationship. The supervisor’s discomfort should be managed separately. Do not make the employee confirm trust, forgiveness, or good character before the concern receives attention.

check.question: What is an appropriate first response?
check.correct: Acknowledge the specific concern, avoid seeking reassurance, and identify the appropriate next step and duties.
wrong: Explain good intentions and close the matter.
Ask the employee to confirm the supervisor is a good person.
Announce that every allegation is now proved.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response receives the concern without defensiveness, unsupported findings, or a burden on the person raising it.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Good intent does not settle effect, reassurance shifts the work to the employee, and receipt is not proof of every fact. Acknowledge the specific concern and identify the next appropriate responsibility with honest limits.

items.text: Name the comment the person is concerned about.
Explain that the concern will receive an appropriate response.
The concern is false because the intent was good.
Receiving the report proves every fact.
Confirm that you still trust me before we continue.
Reassure the supervisor that no harm was meant.

intro.heading: Distinguish what you meant from what the action did
intro.body:
Intent concerns what someone was trying to do. Impact concerns what the action affected. Both can matter, but one does not establish the other. A supervisor may intend to keep a meeting focused while a dismissive comment narrows whose concerns can enter the decision. Explaining the purpose does not examine that effect.

In the practice project meeting, the supervisor says there was a strict deadline. The employee describes hesitating to raise later access questions after being called a distraction in front of colleagues. The deadline is relevant context. The public dismissal and its effect on participation still need attention.

Do not conclude that everyone experienced the comment in the same way or ask the employee to speak for a whole group. Acknowledge the described effect and identify what can be checked or repaired. If facts are uncertain, distinguish that uncertainty from a judgment that the concern is invalid. A careful response can retain the work deadline while changing how access questions are received.

items.title: Separate questions
items.body: Ask what purpose the leader had and what effect the action had on the work. In the meeting case, a deadline may explain urgency, while calling the question a distraction may discourage relevant input. The two statements can coexist. Do not use the first as proof that the second cannot occur.

items.title: Bounded impact
items.body: Describe the effect being raised without claiming a universal experience. The employee reports hesitation to raise later questions; another person may respond differently. That variation does not erase the concern. Examine the participation route and decision effect rather than require a group consensus that the action was harmful.

items.title: Context and responsibility
items.body: Context can help design a feasible repair. If time was constrained, create a clear route for unresolved access questions before the decision closes. This preserves work needs while changing the dismissive response. A deadline explains a condition to manage; it does not authorize humiliating or excluding a contribution.

tabs.label: Intent settles it
tabs.body: Treating intent as the answer can end a conversation before the work effect is examined. It may protect the leader’s explanation while preserving the same participation barrier. Consider context, but still identify what the action did and what needs a response.

tabs.label: Impact with limits
tabs.body: Examining impact with limits recognizes the described effect and identifies remaining uncertainty. It supports a practical change without claiming that everyone had the same reaction. The leader can address the specific behavior and work pathway while an authorized process handles any formal matter.

tabs.label: Universal group claim
tabs.body: A universal group claim makes one employee responsible for representing others and can introduce a stereotype. Different reactions are possible. Examine the concern raised, offer appropriate routes to others, and avoid treating a group vote as necessary proof of harm.

check.question: How should the deadline explanation be used?
check.correct: As context for a feasible response, while still examining the dismissive comment and its effect on participation.
wrong: As proof that no harm occurred.
As a reason to require everyone to share the same reaction.
As evidence that the employee’s concern was disloyal.
check.feedbackCorrect: Context informs the response without replacing examination of the actual effect or imposing a group interpretation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The deadline does not establish harmlessness, uniform experience, or disloyalty. Use it to plan a feasible participation route while examining the specific action and effect rather than dismissing the concern.

items.text: The supervisor wanted to keep the meeting within its deadline.
The supervisor intended to finish the draft discussion.
The employee hesitated to raise later access questions.
The relevant question did not reach the review decision.
Good intent proves that no harm occurred.
Everyone from the same group experienced the comment identically.

options: Use the purpose to close the concern.

responses: Purpose alone does not establish the effect.

The employee is not required to represent a group.

lessons.transfer: Write two separate statements: the intended purpose and the specific effect that needs a response.

move.control: You can distinguish context from the work effect needing attention.
move.failure: A valid work purpose becomes a defense against examining harm.

lessons.title: Clarify without interrogation or forced disclosure
lessons.summary: Write a bounded clarification about an action and its effect.
lessons.objective: Write a bounded clarification about an action and its effect.
objectives: Write a bounded clarification about an action and its effect.
Identify a question that pressures unnecessary personal disclosure.

takeaways: Ask enough to understand the concern within your role.
Do not require a personal history as proof.
Explain limits rather than promise secrecy.
lessons.statement: Clarification should support a response, not test whether someone deserves one.

intro.heading: Clarify without interrogation or forced disclosure
intro.body:
A clarification can help identify the action, relevant context, and effect. It should not become a test of the person’s credibility based on emotional presentation, willingness to disclose identity, or ability to educate the leader. Ask what is needed for the next appropriate responsibility and avoid gathering unrelated personal information.

In the practice case, the supervisor can ask which part of the meeting response caused the concern and what happened to the access question afterward. Demanding a detailed account of every past experience, or asking why the employee did not object publicly, adds pressure without necessarily helping the work response.

Choose an appropriate setting and explain information limits. A leader should not promise that nothing can leave the conversation if a report requires another authorized office. Do not place actual complaint, employee, or participant records in a learning exercise. If the concern requires formal reporting, fulfill that duty; a private clarification is not a prerequisite for the route.

Identify a question that pressures unnecessary personal disclosure.

What should the supervisor do instead?
lessons.keyStatement: Clarification should support a response, not test whether someone deserves one.

items.title: Useful question
items.body: A useful question connects directly to the action and next responsibility. In the meeting case, ask what happened to the access concern after the dismissal and whether there is an unresolved design issue. This gives the leader a practical path to act without asking the employee to supply a complete personal history.

items.title: Pressure
items.body: Asking why the employee was not more assertive shifts attention away from the leader’s response and may make public confrontation a hidden requirement. A person can raise a concern later or through another appropriate route. Do not equate a calm tone, delayed report, or limited disclosure with lack of validity.

items.title: Information limits
items.body: Explain who may need relevant information and avoid collecting more than your role requires. The leader cannot guarantee absolute secrecy or improvise an investigation outside assigned agency procedures or authority. Assigned investigation responsibilities remain governed by agency procedures and the authorized role. Use the appropriate process for formal concerns and preserve information appropriately rather than turn the employee’s account into a group learning example.

tabs.label: Focused clarification
tabs.body: Focused clarification can reveal the work action and next step with less unnecessary disclosure. It should remain within the leader’s role and should not delay required reporting. The person may choose not to provide every detail in an informal conversation; explain the appropriate available route.

tabs.label: Credibility test
tabs.body: A credibility test based on assertiveness, emotion, or personal history can make receipt depend on the leader’s expectations of the person. It does not establish the facts. Keep the question connected to the concern and use an authorized process for matters requiring investigation.

tabs.label: Secrecy promise
tabs.body: A secrecy promise may encourage disclosure but can conflict with reporting or records responsibilities. State accurate limits before gathering information. Privacy means appropriate handling and sharing, not an unsupported guarantee that no authorized person will ever need the information.

check.question: Which clarification is appropriate?
check.correct: Ask about the specific meeting response and what happened to the access question, with accurate process and privacy limits.
wrong: Require all past personal experiences before responding.
Ask why the employee did not confront the supervisor publicly.
Promise no information can ever leave the conversation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The question supports a bounded work response without forcing disclosure or offering inaccurate guarantees.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A personal-history demand, a confrontation test, and absolute secrecy can each create a barrier. Ask about the specific action and effect within your role, explain limits, and use the proper route without making an informal explanation mandatory.

items.text: Which part of the response are you concerned about?
What happened to the access question after the meeting?
List every prior harmful experience before I respond.
Prove the concern by confronting the supervisor publicly.
Relevant information may need the appropriate authorized office.
Do not put real complaint records in this course exercise.

lessons.transfer: Prepare one bounded question, one accurate privacy limit, and a proper route if formal responsibility applies.

move.control: You can keep clarification necessary, respectful, and within role.
move.failure: An understanding conversation becomes a test or a collection of unnecessary personal information.

lessons.title: Take responsibility without demanding forgiveness
lessons.summary: Draft an apology for a specific action without a defensive condition.
lessons.objective: Draft an apology for a specific action without a defensive condition.
objectives: Draft an apology for a specific action without a defensive condition.
Distinguish accurate personal responsibility from an unsupported formal finding.
Identify a repair that does not require forgiveness, reassurance, or complaint withdrawal.
takeaways: Name the action rather than apologize for the person’s reaction.
An apology needs a credible next action.
Forgiveness is not a condition or outcome measure.
lessons.statement: Take responsibility for the action you can accurately identify.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Take responsibility without demanding forgiveness
intro.body:
A useful apology identifies a specific action and takes responsibility for it. An apology for someone being offended can leave the behavior unaddressed. A long explanation of good intent can also turn the response into a defense. Keep the acknowledgment accurate and connect it to a practical change within your authority.

In the practice case, the supervisor can apologize for publicly dismissing the access concern and explain that relevant questions will receive a substantive response. The supervisor should not promise an investigative finding or ask the employee to affirm that trust is restored. A personal apology and any required formal process are distinct responsibilities.

The person can decline a conversation, remain dissatisfied, or use an available reporting route. Do not make a repair conditional on accepting the apology, withdrawing a complaint, or providing reassurance. The leader’s follow-through is under the leader’s control. Whether the person forgives or feels differently is not an outcome the leader can require or declare.

inThisLesson: Draft an apology for a specific action without a defensive condition.
Distinguish accurate personal responsibility from an unsupported formal finding.
Identify a repair that does not require forgiveness, reassurance, or complaint withdrawal.
What should change?
lessons.keyStatement: Take responsibility for the action you can accurately identify.

items.title: Specific ownership
items.body: Name what you did accurately. In the meeting case, the supervisor can own calling the access question a distraction in front of the team. This differs from an apology only for the employee’s feelings. Specific ownership gives the repair a clear target without making a finding about every allegation or another person’s motive.

items.title: Credible change
items.body: Connect the apology to an action that can be implemented, such as reviewing the unresolved question and changing how concerns are received. Avoid an absolute promise that no harm will ever occur again. A credible change has responsibility and review, while a sweeping promise cannot be verified.

items.title: No exchange
items.body: Do not exchange a repair for forgiveness, silence, or withdrawal. The leader should address the action because it is a responsibility, not because the person agrees to close the concern. A report or ongoing dissatisfaction can remain while a practical repair occurs through appropriate authority and information boundaries.

tabs.label: Conditional apology
tabs.body: A conditional apology can seem polite while implying that the problem is the employee’s reaction. It may not identify any action the leader will change. Name the behavior accurately and avoid a condition that the person must accept the leader’s explanation.

tabs.label: Specific apology and action
tabs.body: A specific apology acknowledges an action and connects it to a feasible change. It does not promise universal trust or decide a formal outcome. This makes the leader’s responsibility visible and gives follow-up something practical to examine.

tabs.label: Forgiveness requirement
tabs.body: A forgiveness requirement can pressure the person to perform closure so the leader can report success. The leader cannot require that experience. Review whether the repair was implemented and keep appropriate routes open regardless of whether the apology is accepted.

check.question: Which apology addresses the leader’s action?
check.correct: “I am sorry I publicly dismissed the access concern. I will ensure it receives an appropriate review and change how I respond to work concerns.”
wrong: “I am sorry if you chose to be offended.”
“I will repair it only if you confirm trust is restored.”
“My apology means the formal matter is now closed.”
check.feedbackCorrect: The apology names the specific action and a next responsibility without blaming the reaction, demanding forgiveness, or claiming formal closure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An apology about the person’s reaction avoids ownership. Requiring trust or declaring formal closure exceeds the leader’s control. Name the action accurately, plan a credible change, and preserve the person’s options and the appropriate process.

items.text: Own the public dismissal of the access question.
Avoid making the employee’s reaction the fault.
Assign review of the unresolved access concern.
Change how later work questions receive a response.
Accept the apology before a repair begins.
Withdraw the report to demonstrate teamwork.

options: Keep the conditions to make the result measurable.

responses: The conditions measure pressured closure rather than the leader’s work.

lessons.transfer: Write a specific apology, a feasible next action, and a sentence preserving appropriate options.

move.control: You can own your action and carry out a credible repair.
move.failure: An apology becomes an exchange for forgiveness or silence.

lessons.objective: Identify a concern that requires an authorized formal response.
objectives: Identify a concern that requires an authorized formal response.

intro.heading: Use the appropriate route while repairing the work
intro.body:
Some concerns about harm can be addressed through a practical change in ordinary work. Others involve allegations requiring reporting, investigation, immediate assistance, or another authorized responsibility. The leader should examine the substance and applicable policy rather than decide that an apology makes the formal route unnecessary.

In a practice variation, the employee says the dismissal was accompanied by repeated remarks about a protected characteristic. Under the applicable state policy, managers must immediately report allegations of harassment or discrimination through HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. The leader should not delay that duty until after a private conversation or consultant review.

The project may still need appropriate work coordination and correction of the unresolved access issue. Keep those actions distinct from determining facts, assigning discipline, or promising a formal outcome. Do not retaliate, require reconciliation, or restrict the person’s reporting options. The consultant can offer guidance and feedback while staff and leaders fulfill their own responsibilities through the proper routes.

inThisLesson: Identify a concern that requires an authorized formal response.
Explain why personal repair does not replace a manager’s reporting duty.
Plan operational coordination that avoids investigating or imposing conditions outside your role.
What should happen?
lessons.keyStatement: A personal response cannot waive a responsibility to use the proper process.

items.title: Duty
items.body: A report’s substance may require a particular response even when the leader did not witness the action or intends to apologize. In the protected-characteristic case, the manager’s immediate reporting duty is separate from personal repair. Do not delay required reporting for an improvised investigation or wait for the person to accept an apology. Any assigned investigation duties must follow agency procedures and the authorized role.

items.title: Role
items.body: Coordinate the work within your authority and use the proper office for formal matters. A supervisor can preserve the unresolved access question and plan an appropriate review without making an investigative finding. Avoid collecting excessive records, directing witnesses, or assigning discipline through a team-learning conversation.

items.title: Support
items.body: Consultant guidance can help a leader think through a response and build capability. It cannot become permission to use HR, the Affirmative Action Officer, or another appropriate process. Staff should retain their options. Explain the correct route and fulfill your responsibility instead of transferring the decision to a consultant gate.

tabs.label: Apology as closure
tabs.body: An apology can acknowledge a known action but does not determine a formal matter or remove reporting duties. Calling it closure may pressure the person and leave the required response undone. Separate personal responsibility, work repair, and the authorized process.

tabs.label: Appropriate parallel action
tabs.body: Appropriate parallel action fulfills the reporting duty and coordinates a bounded work repair. It requires clear role and information limits. A corrected participation route can be useful without claiming that the formal issue is resolved or that all findings are established.

tabs.label: Consultant gate
tabs.body: A consultant gate can appear supportive while delaying access and shifting responsibility away from the leader. Use guidance as support rather than permission. The applicable reporting route and manager’s duties remain available regardless of whether a consultation has occurred.

check.question: What should a manager do when the concern includes alleged protected-class remarks?
check.correct: Immediately use the appropriate agency reporting route and keep any personal repair and work coordination appropriately bounded.
wrong: Wait until the employee accepts an apology.
Ask the consultant whether a report is allowed.
Decide the finding in a team conversation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response fulfills the applicable responsibility without replacing it with personal repair, a gate, or an unauthorized finding.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Apology acceptance and consultant permission are not prerequisites for the manager’s duty. A team conversation also cannot decide the finding. Use the appropriate route promptly and keep operational repair within authority and privacy limits.

items.text: Immediately report the allegation through the appropriate agency route.
Cooperate with the authorized process as required.
Review the unresolved access question through proper work authority.
Explain necessary coordination without sharing private details.
The apology replaces an investigation.
Consultant approval is required before HR access.

lessons.title: Review the repair without scoring the person’s response
lessons.summary: Choose evidence that a specific work repair was implemented.
lessons.objective: Choose evidence that a specific work repair was implemented.
objectives: Choose evidence that a specific work repair was implemented.
Distinguish process improvement from proof of forgiveness or restored trust.

takeaways: Check the action and its effect on the work.
Silence or acceptance does not prove restored trust.
Keep unresolved concerns and appropriate options visible.
lessons.statement: Measure follow-through rather than require a performance of forgiveness.

intro.heading: Review the repair without scoring the person’s response
intro.body:
Follow-through should examine whether the agreed action occurred and whether it addressed the work effect. Did the access question receive a substantive review? Was there a usable route for later concerns? Was the leader’s response practice changed? These are reviewable questions. They do not establish every employee’s experience or produce a validated measure of trust.

In the practice project, the access question reaches the authorized person and a missing assumption is corrected before the next draft. That shows a specific repair in the work. The employee may still remain cautious about speaking publicly or continue through a formal route. The leader should not treat that caution as refusal to collaborate.

Do not rank employees by how quickly they accept an apology, return to visible participation, or stop raising concerns. Keep follow-up bounded, protect information, and explain what remains uncertain. If the action failed or created another barrier, revise it through appropriate authority. A credible response continues with responsibility rather than asking the person to certify that the leader has improved.

inThisLesson: Choose evidence that a specific work repair was implemented.
Distinguish process improvement from proof of forgiveness or restored trust.
Plan follow-up that preserves unresolved concerns and avoids individual emotional scores.
What should the review focus on?
lessons.keyStatement: Measure follow-through rather than require a performance of forgiveness.

items.title: Implementation evidence
items.body: Check whether the access concern was reviewed and the decision record reflects the answer. This establishes use of the repair for a specific issue. Compare it with the intended action and identify a missed responsibility or timing problem. Do not use a completed apology meeting as proof that the work effect changed.

items.title: Effect and limits
items.body: The corrected assumption may improve the draft, but does not prove that trust is restored or all later input routes work. Describe the bounded result and remaining questions. If broader climate evidence is used, follow appropriate design, privacy, and interpretation practices rather than invent a score from one conversation.

items.title: Follow-up without pressure
items.body: Ask about the work action and explain the route for continuing concerns without requiring emotional closure. A person can remain dissatisfied and still contribute professionally. Do not create a special participation watch after feedback or interpret caution as disloyalty. Review the leader’s practice and relevant process instead.

tabs.label: Apology attendance
tabs.body: Attendance is an activity measure and may reflect pressure, choice, or a desire to resolve the work. It does not establish that the repair was useful or that trust returned. Examine the specific action and decision effect rather than report the meeting itself as success.

tabs.label: Work-path review
tabs.body: A work-path review checks the concern from receipt to action and follow-up. It can reveal whether the repair addressed the practical barrier. Its limits should remain explicit; one corrected issue does not establish every person’s experience or a universal improvement.

tabs.label: Forgiveness score
tabs.body: A forgiveness score asks the person to certify the leader’s success and can penalize an honest continuing concern. The leader cannot require that feeling. Track responsibility, implementation, and appropriate work effects without ranking the person’s response to an apology.

check.question: What does the corrected assumption establish?
check.correct: A specific work issue received review and correction, while trust and broader experience remain separate and limited conclusions.
wrong: The employee must now forgive the supervisor.
All staff trust the leader again.
A continuing report means the repair failed completely.
check.feedbackCorrect: The evidence supports a bounded work result without requiring emotional closure or deciding the status of a formal matter.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Forgiveness and universal trust do not follow from a corrected draft, and a continuing report has a separate purpose. Describe the specific action and effect, explain limits, and preserve appropriate options rather than score the employee’s reaction.

sections.heading: Receive and understand
items: Pause defensiveness and acknowledge the specific concern.
Ask a bounded clarification without demanding a personal history.
Separate what is known, what is described, and what needs an authorized review.

sections.heading: Respond appropriately
items: Own a specific action you can accurately identify.
Explain the applicable route and fulfill your duties.
Choose a practical repair without requiring withdrawal, reconciliation, or silence.

sections.heading: Check follow-through
items: Assign the change, timing, and review responsibility.
Protect information and preserve appropriate reporting access.
Review whether the work changed without scoring the person’s forgiveness or feelings.
